title: Listen (Rule, Prologue)
hook: the Rule's first word: listen, my son, with the ear of your heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, a block close: a family that disagrees and still says one creed. Your line was many rooms, one house.

Ausculta. That's the first word of a short book for monks, written in Latin by a man the church remembers as Saint Benedict. It's called simply the Rule. Before it says a thing about prayer times, food, sleep or work, it says one word. Listen. Not read carefully. Not obey. Listen. And not only with the ears on the side of your head: the opening line asks the reader, as a son, to listen to the teacher's instruction and bend down the ear of the heart. A new block starts today, traditions of prayer, the different ways Christians have learned to pray, and the first house is the Benedictines.

The ear of the heart is an odd phrase, and it's meant to be. An ear hears sounds. This ear goes further in: listening all the way down, willing to be changed by what it hears. The picture is an old one. In Proverbs, a parent says, "My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings." Incline. Lean the ear over, the way you lean toward someone speaking softly in a loud room. A little further on, the Prologue reaches for a psalm about listening too: "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart." Today. Not someday when life is quieter. Now notice what the Rule takes for granted. In its picture, God is already speaking, through scripture, the teacher, the community, the day as it comes, and the trouble is mostly on the listener's end. People are busy. They rehearse their answer. They hear half a sentence and fill in the rest. So the Rule doesn't start with a technique. It starts with a posture: lean in, bend down, leave room for a voice that isn't yours. Prayer times, food, sleep and work all come after. A whole way of life, built on one verb, and anyone can practice it, with or without a cloister: at a kitchen table, in a meeting, on the phone with your mother.
screen: `AN EAR THAT GOES ALL THE WAY IN.`
`TO DAY IF YE WILL HEAR HIS VOICE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'll talk with today, and see their face. Picture the conversation and notice the moment you usually start forming your reply while they're still talking; decide to let them finish, lean in a little, and ask one more question before you answer. If you pray, ask for an ear of the heart; if you don't, just hold the person in mind and rest.
Listen. The first word of Benedict's Rule: ausculta, hearing with the ear of the heart.
Your line: the ear of the heart. Ausculta: one word, and a life built on it. That's today, done.

howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the Rule is read aloud to the community in short passages, and each time through it begins again with the Prologue's call to listen; lay people who follow Benedictine ways, called oblates, may read the Rule at home as well.

chat.says: Why would a whole rule for monks start with the word listen?
options: Because in the Rule God is already speaking; the trouble is our hurry, so it starts with leaning in.
Because monks weren't allowed to speak at all, so listening was the only thing left to them.
Because the Rule was read aloud, and listen there only means pay attention to the reader.
chat.meaning: The Rule assumes God is already speaking, through scripture, the teacher, the community and the day. So it begins with a posture: bend down the ear of the heart.

notes: The Rule is paraphrased throughout (no public-domain English translation on the approved list). The Latin opening 'Ausculta, o fili, praecepta magistri, et inclina aurem cordis tui' is the basis for 'listen, my son... ear of the heart'; please confirm the paraphrase.
Proverbs 4:20 is offered as the scriptural picture behind 'incline'; commentators link the opening to Proverbs. Confirm this is fair to say ('he's borrowing the voice of Proverbs').
The Prologue's use of Psalm 95 (Vulgate 94) 'today if you hear his voice' is cited as Prologue 9–10; check numbering.
'Benedictines still read from the Rule in their communities' and the oblate line in howItsDone are general descriptions not in the cited text; confirm or soften.
No date for Benedict is given, under the claims rule.
